Subject: Please read and share – fake blue pills and when to call 999

I’m posting this separately because the police warning is on here but it’s getting lost, and the thread about Saturday is mostly rumours and people slagging kids off. This is general safety information, not a comment on any individual or on what may or may not have happened.

The police are warning about blue tablets being sold as diazepam or “Xanax”. Some have been found to contain nitazenes – synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. You cannot tell what is in one of these tablets just by looking at it.

Warning signs include extreme drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, slow or noisy breathing, and blue lips.

If someone has taken something and becomes unwell, call 999 straight away. If your mate goes down, don’t put them to bed to “sleep it off”. Don’t leave them alone and ring hours later. Stay with them and follow the call handler’s instructions. Someone who looks as though they’re just sleeping may be breathing dangerously slowly. Waiting can mean their brain has gone without oxygen for too long.

And please don’t delay because you’re frightened of getting into trouble. The police have said clearly: “Our priority is preserving life.” Getting help is the right thing to do.

Naloxone nasal spray can reverse the effects of opioids. It doesn’t replace calling 999, but it’s worth knowing about and having. Brightpath drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette, provides free nasal naloxone kits. Anyone can ask and no names are needed. Training takes about ten minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday, 10am–4pm, with Thursday opening until 7pm.

Parents, please talk to your teenagers this week – not after half term or when you next get round to it. I had the chat with my own lad last night over his tea. There were plenty of eye rolls, but he listened, and he asked me what pinpoint pupils meant. That’s exactly why we need to have these conversations, even when we think our kids already know or would never take anything.

Make sure they know what to do for a friend: ring 999 immediately, don’t leave them in bed, and don’t let fear of a row stop them calling.

And please, enough of the blame. Frightened kids who think they’ll be judged or get into trouble are exactly the ones who won’t ring for help. Slagging them or their parents off helps nobody. Whatever anyone thinks about drugs, that cannot matter more than a young person’s life.

Please share this post rather than just liking it, and make sure the teenagers and parents in your life actually read it.
